summary: Describes conventions for using cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax to protect the symmetric key package content type, covering SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData and AuthEnvelopedData. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of which locks and seals to use when mailing a package of secret keys.

which algorithms must cms authenvelopeddata support
subtitle: Which signature, key transport and key wrap algorithms to support when CMS protects symmetric key packages.

tldr.problem: The symmetric key package content type needs protection in CMS, and implementers need to know which algorithms to support for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists MUST and SHOULD algorithms for SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData and AuthEnvelopedData, plus minimum public key sizes, without defining any new algorithm.
tldr.outcome: Implementations share a common baseline built on RSA, AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding and AES-GCM.

today: RFC 6160 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement or update.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
This document gives conventions for using cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 5652) to protect the symmetric key package content type defined in RFC 6031. It covers four CMS content types: SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData and AuthEnvelopedData (RFC 5083).

It defines no new algorithms; it points to previously defined ones.
sections.plainLanguage: It does not invent new locks. It just says which existing locks to use.

sections.title: Signing and Encrypting Algorithms
sections.content:
For SignedData, an implementation MUST support RSA and SHOULD support RSASSA-PSS and DSA, and SHA-256 MUST be supported alongside them while SHA-1 SHOULD be. ECDSA is a MAY.

For EnvelopedData, key transport MUST be implemented and key agreement MAY be. RSA encryption MUST be supported for transport and RSAES-OAEP SHOULD be. For key agreement, ephemeral-static Diffie-Hellman MUST be supported and ECDH MAY be. Either way, AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding MUST be supported as the content-encryption algorithm and AES-256 SHOULD be. With key agreement, the same key-wrap algorithm MUST be used for key and content encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a list of must-have and nice-to-have locks for signing and for sealing packages. Everyone has to carry the must-haves.

sections.title: EncryptedData, AuthEnvelopedData and Key Sizes
sections.content:
EncryptedData MUST use AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding and SHOULD support AES-256. Keys are managed by other means, so only the content-encryption algorithm is specified.

AuthEnvelopedData follows the EnvelopedData rules except that the content-encryption algorithm MUST be AES-GCM: 128-bit MUST be implemented and 256-bit SHOULD be. AES-CCM is a MAY.

For public keys, RSA, RSASSA-PSS, DSA, RSAES-OAEP and Diffie-Hellman implementations MUST support key lengths from 1024-bit to 2048-bit inclusive. ECDSA and ECDH implementations MUST support keys on P-256.
sections.plainLanguage: Different kinds of envelopes each get their own required lock, and the keys must be at least a certain size.

sections.title: Security Reasoning
sections.content:
The security considerations of the referenced CMS and algorithm RFCs apply. The content-encryption choice follows RFC 5649: a mechanism used solely for protecting keying material helps in high assurance cryptographic modules that keep keys separate from other data.

No AES-GCM or AES-CCM mode provides the same properties; if one is defined, this document will be updated to adopt it. NIST SP 800-57 gives comparable bits of security and time frames that some environments may find useful.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys get a special lock used only for keys, so they stay apart from ordinary data.
